analysis.one_liner: Limits courts' power to seal evidence of public health and safety hazards in lawsuit settlements.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill with bipartisan support in May 2011, but it sat on the Senate calendar and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies facing lawsuits over dangerous products often settle on condition that the evidence of the hazard stays secret, and courts routinely approve those confidential settlements. This bill would tell federal courts they may not seal such information, or block a party from telling a safety regulator about it, unless the judge first finds on the record that secrecy serves a specific, substantial interest and goes no further than needed. Settlement secrecy about personal financial or medical details would stay protected.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people harmed by unsafe drugs, cars, or consumer products, because evidence of hazards uncovered in lawsuits could no longer routinely be hidden by confidential settlements. It also helps regulators, journalists, and future litigants, who would gain access to information about past, present, and potential health or safety hazards [S2][S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and patients endangered by unsafe products

how_it_helps.text: In any lawsuit where the pleadings raise facts relevant to public health or safety, a court could not seal discovery information, approve a settlement that hides such information, or restrict access to court records unless it first makes independent findings that secrecy would not block health-and-safety information, or that the public's interest in learning of hazards is outweighed by a specific and substantial confidentiality interest and the order is no broader than necessary [S3][S4].

Courts could not approve or enforce any agreement provision stopping a party from disclosing relevant information to a federal or state agency with authority to enforce laws on the subject, and could not enforce settlement terms that bar a party from saying a settlement was reached, describing its terms (other than the amount paid), or discussing the evidence in the case [S2][S4].
The party asking for secrecy carries the burden of proof, and the bill includes a rebuttable presumption protecting individuals' personal financial and health information from disclosure [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Defendant companies in product-liability, drug, medical device, and other health-and-safety litigation, which would lose the ability to buy peace with settlements that keep hazard evidence out of public view. Courts and parties would also bear the cost of the extra on-the-record findings secrecy now requires [S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the usual flexibility judges and parties have under Rule 26(c) to keep litigation confidential: even when both sides of a health-or-safety case agree to settle quietly, a court could not enforce that confidentiality without formal findings that public disclosure interests are outweighed [S3][S4].

Removing confidentiality can make companies less willing to settle quickly, which can mean longer cases and smaller or slower recoveries for some injured plaintiffs; the bill itself acknowledges the privacy stakes by presuming that individuals' personal financial and health information should stay confidential [S4].
Committee Republicans filed minority views with the report, signaling that the panel's minority saw problems with the approach even as the bill was reported favorably [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: more public information about hazards versus somewhat less settlement flexibility and more court paperwork. The bill is carefully built for this trade — it keeps settlements confidential when a judge finds a specific, substantial reason, protects personal financial and health details with a presumption, and never reaches classified information or intelligence sources and methods [S3][S4]. The drawbacks are procedural costs and slower settlements, not a loss of safety protection.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of business, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Herb Kohl introduced the Sunshine in Litigation Act of 2011 on March 17, 2011, joined by Sens. Graham, Leahy, and Feinstein, and it was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee [S1][S4][S6].

On May 19, 2011, the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 64 [S6].

The reported version added explicit protections for classified information and intelligence sources and methods, and barred using the new law to reopen protective or settlement orders entered before enactment [S3][S4].
On August 2, 2011, the committee filed its written report (Report No. 112-45), with minority views filed; no further action followed for the rest of the Congress [S6].
The bill never received a Senate floor vote and died on January 3, 2013, when the 112th Congress ended [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defendant companies benefit from the outcome: they keep the ability to resolve safety-hazard lawsuits with court-approved settlements that seal the evidence. Nothing about public access to hazard information changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defendant companies that seal hazard evidence

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — sponsored by a Democrat with a Republican cosponsor and two other Democrats, and reported favorably by a Democratic chair — though the committee's Republicans filed minority views, and the Senate as a whole never voted [S4][S5][S6].

industries.industry: Product-liability defendants (drug and device makers, automakers, consumer product manufacturers)
industries.note: These companies routinely use confidential settlements that seal evidence of health and safety hazards; the bill would let courts approve such secrecy only after specific findings, and would bar enforcing gag terms that block disclosure to regulators. Their interest in keeping settlements quiet runs directly against the public's interest in learning about hazards.

Hazard evidence would be harder to seal, which can strengthen future cases and public awareness, but individual plaintiffs who personally want a confidential settlement — including for their own medical or financial details — would face limits, cushioned by the bill's privacy presumption.

The bill guarantees that parties can disclose relevant information to any agency with authority to enforce related laws, giving regulators access to hazard evidence that secret settlements currently keep from them.
